lines.text: Your crops are dying in the sun, and the river is right there, just below the bank.
So you climb down with a bucket, fill it, and haul it back up the bank, over and over.
But by noon you have watered three rows, and your back is screaming.
So you plant a tall forked post right at the edge of the bank.
Lay a long pole in the fork, tied a fifth of the way from one end, like a seesaw.
Hang the bucket from the long end on a rope, and pull it down into the river.
But lifting a full bucket on the end of a pole is just as hard as carrying it.
So you pack wet mud into a big ball on the short end and let it bake hard in the sun.
Now the ball wants to fall, and when it falls, it lifts the bucket for you. This is a counterweight.
Pull the empty bucket down, let the weight swing it up full, then turn the pole and tip it out.
This is a shaduf. One person can lift about two thousand liters of water an hour.
But the water just soaks into the dirt right where you pour it.
So you dig a channel along the top of the bank, lined with packed clay, with furrows branching between your rows.
Every bucket now runs straight to the roots. This is an irrigation canal.
But your bucket leaks half its water on the way up.
So you weave a basket out of reeds and coat it in sticky black tar, so it holds every drop.
Farmers in Mesopotamia were lifting water like this over four thousand years ago, and some still do today.
Congratulations. You have built a shaduf.
